title: Infections of the Liver and Biliary System

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of fever, chills, nausea, anorexia, myalgia, and fatigue. She had a history of colorectal cancer with biliary obstruction. She had no drug allergies. Investigations: Total white cell count 16,000/mm3 Bicarbonate 19 mmol/L Lactate 1.9 mmol/L Bilirubin 5.5 mg/dL Abdominal imaging revealed multiple collections in the liver, consistent with metastases versus abscesses. One of the larger lesions was aspirated, revealing frank purulence. Cultures of this abscess were positive for Citrobacter freundii and Enterococcus faecalis , antibiotic sensitivities pending.
questions.lead_in: What empiric monotherapy agent would be most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Imipenem–cilastatin Neither sulbactam or tazobactam reliably inhibit AmpC beta-lactamases that Citrobacter freundii is known to produce. Ertapenem is inactive against enterococci, and meropenem possesses only marginal activity against Enterococcus faecalis. Imipenem–cilastatin is stable to AmpC betalactamases produced by Citrobacter freundii and is also reliably active against Enterococcus faecalis.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q5

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man was seen with a history of intermittent fevers over 6 weeks. He denied any other symptoms. He was being investigated for raised blood sugars and had a dental extraction 7 days earlier. He drank 35 units of alcohol per week. He returned from Malaysia 6 months ago following a 2-month stay with his family during the summer months. On examination, his temperature was 38.9°C, and he had mild abdominal tenderness in his right upper quadrant. Investigations: Total white cell count 17.2 ×109/L CRP 230 mg/L Alanine transaminase 152 U/L Alkaline phosphatase 341 U/L Urgent abdominal USS revealed a single large lesion in the right lobe of the liver consistent with an abscess. No biliary pathology was identified. He was commenced on fluids and IV co-amoxiclav Blood cultures – no growth at 5 days Liver aspirate MCS – mucoid colonies on blood and MacConkey agar. The organism did not react with oxidase or indole A B
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Klebsiella pneumoniae K. pneumoniae (K1 capsular serotype) is an emerging pathogen causing liver abscesses in the absence of hepatobiliary disease. It is found in SE Asia, in particular Malaysia. K. pneumoniae are oxidase-negative, lactose fermenting organism. The hypermucoviscous variant grows as very mucoid colonies and can be identified by a positive string test (stretching colonies forms a “string” of >5mm). E. coli is a common causes of liver abscess, and the culture results would fit (although most E. coli are indole positive) but in the absence of hepatobiliary pathology and sterile blood cultures this would be unlikely. E. histolytica commonly presents as an indolent infection and is endemic in rural areas of Malaysia. Against this diagnosis is no preceding colitis (one third) and Entamoeba do not grow on blood or MacConkey agar as they require supplemented media (usually egg yolk). Melioidosis, caused by B. pseudomallei , is a condition causing large abscesses. B. pseudomallei is an environmental saprophyte found in aquatic environments and when cultured grows as mucoid colonies. Going against this as a diagnosis is that infections are most prevalent following the rainy season (rather than summer months when the patient traveled). Also, while it can be found in Malaysia is it more prevalent in Thailand and North Australia. Furthermore, B. pseudomallei are oxidase-positive. Streptococcus intermedius is one of the S. milleri group, which are well recognized as causing deep-seated abscesses such as this. However, the colonial appearances on blood agar are not consistent with S. intermedius, and MacConkey agar does not support its growth. (Image ( left) reprinted with permission from Elsevier. The Lancet. From Prokesch BC, et al. Primary osteomyelitis caused by hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae. Lancet Infect Dis. 2016;16(9):e190–e195. Image ( right) from Rath S, Padhy RN. Prevalence of two multidrug-resistant Klebsiella species in an Indian teaching hospital and adjoining community. J Infect Public Health. 2014;7(6):496–507.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q20

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man presented in status epilepticus. He was usually fit and well and had returned 1 week earlier from a 2-month visit to Taiwan to visit family. He had no history of recent hospital admission or attendance. He did not take any regular medications, nor did he use any recreational drugs. On examination he had a temperature of 38.3°C, and his pulse was 110 beats/minute. He was sedated, intubated, and transferred to critical care following an urgent CT scan with contrast. Empirical treatment with ceftriaxone and metronidazole was commenced. Investigations: White cell count 23.1 ×109/L (4–11) Neutrophil count 21.8 ×109/L (2–7.5) C-reactive protein 245 mg/L (0–5) Alkaline phosphatase 197 U/L (40–129) ALT 50 U/L (0–41) Total bilirubin 13 μmol/L (0–21) CT head: Liver USS: The liver is heterogenous and mildly enlarged. In the left lobe there is a 79 × 71 × 58mm well-circumscribed, heterogenous area with no vascularity; ? liver abscess
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Klebsiella pneumoniae The patient has both cerebral abscesses (ring-enhancing lesions) and a liver abscess. There is a systemic inflammatory response with fever, neutrophilia, and raised C-reactive protein. There is a recognized association of primary liver abscesses caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae with hematogenous spread leading to cerebral abscesses. The travel history should be elicited as there is a higher incidence in SE Asia. (Image from Prayson RA, Neuropathology, 2nd ed. Saunders; 2012.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q3

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man presented with a 4-day history of high-grade fever and chills. He had undergone liver transplantation for primary sclerosing cholangitis 3 weeks earlier. He was maintained on tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and prednisone. Investigations: Recipient CMV IgG negative, donor CMV IgG negative Total white cell count 20.1 ×109/L Alkaline phosphatase 406 IU/L
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Increase immunosuppression for acute cellular rejection
Reduce immunosuppression for drug-induced liver injury
Start empirical ganciclovir for presumed CMV disease
Start empirical ivAB for intraabdominal infection

questions.explanation: Start empirical ivAB for intraabdominal infection Intraabdominal and biliary complications after liver transplant range from biliary leaks and bilomas to ascending cholangitis and liver abscess from biliary strictures resulting from hepatic artery thrombosis. These patients can present without right upper quadrant pain or tenderness because of allograft denervation. CMV disease is unlikely given leukocytosis and D−/R− status, and invasive aspergillosis is unlikely given early presentation posttransplant and the absence of neutropenia. Surgical complication or intraabdominal infection should be suspected, empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics started, and the abdomen imaged.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q24

questions.question: Regarding the pathophysiology of pyogenic liver abscesses.
questions.question_raw: 22. Regarding the pathophysiology of pyogenic liver abscesses

parts.text: List 4 different causal mechanisms.

parts_raw.text: List 4 different causal mechanisms

questions.model_answer: (1) Biliary tract disease with ascending/contiguous spread (cholangitis, obstruction) — now the major underlying cause. (2) Portal venous seeding (pylephlebitis) from an intra-abdominal infection such as diverticulitis or appendicitis. (3) Hepatic arterial (hematogenous) seeding from systemic bacteremia/intravascular infection. (4) Direct extension from a contiguous focus or penetrating trauma (a fifth, cryptogenic, accounts for the remainder).

cohort_answer.text: Portal vein pyemia, usually related to bowel leakage and peritonitis; Direct spread from biliary infection (gallstones, malignant obstruction); Surgical or penetrating wounds, including migration of ingested foreign body; Hematogenous seeding from systemic circulation.

questions.question: A patient presents with a pyogenic liver abscess and has never travelled.

parts.text: Name 3 of the most common clinical manifestations.
Name the 2 most common Gram-positive organisms, the 2 most common Gram-negative organisms, and the most common anaerobe.

parts_raw.text: A) Most common clinical manifestation (name 3)
B) 2 most common gram +, two most common gram -, most common anaerobe?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Fever (~80%). (2) Abdominal pain. (3) Anorexia/weight loss (malaise, failure to thrive); RUQ tenderness and jaundice are less consistent. b) Gram-positive: Streptococcus anginosus group and Enterococcus spp. Gram-negative: Escherichia coli and Klebsiella spp. (the two most common overall). Anaerobe: Bacteroides spp.

cohort_answer.text:
Fever; Abdominal pain; Anorexia/weight loss
Gram +: Strep anginosus group and Enterococcus most common, also S. aureus, GAS. Gram -: Klebsiella, E coli. Anaerobe: Bacteroides

questions.question: A 35-year-old man presents with fever and abdominal pain. Imaging is consistent with a pyogenic liver abscess. The lesion is aspirated and pus is retrieved.
questions.question_raw:
Q51 (2016 AM)
35M presents with fever and abdominal pain. Imaging is consistent with a pyogenic liver abscess. The lesion is aspirated and pus is retrieved.

parts.text: Name 4 pathogenic mechanisms for formation of a pyogenic liver abscess.

parts_raw.text: A) Name 4 pathogenic mechanisms for formation of a pyogenic liver abscess

questions.model_answer: (1) Biliary spread (ascending cholangitis/biliary obstruction) — the leading underlying cause. (2) Portal venous seeding (pylephlebitis) from an intra-abdominal source such as diverticulitis or appendicitis. (3) Hepatic arterial (hematogenous) seeding from systemic bacteremia. (4) Direct/contiguous extension or penetrating trauma (cryptogenic accounts for the remaining cases).

cohort_answer.text: Direct extension (e.g. trauma or fishbone from GI tract); Venous extension (e.g. colitis/diverticulitis); Biliary extension (e.g. cholangitis, stricture); Arterial extension (e.g. hematogenous); Local extension (e.g. empyema, perinephric abscess, peritonitis); Cryptogenic

questions.question: [image-based question: patient with multiple abscesses growing a gram-negative rod, with a photo of a plate showing a positive string test.]
questions.question_raw: [image-based question: Patient with multiple abscesses growing GNR with photo of a plate with positive string test.]

parts.text: Name the organism and serotype.
Give four mechanisms for liver abscess pathogenesis.
Give two virulence factors for this organism.

parts_raw.text: Name the organism and serotype.
Four mechanisms for liver abscess pathogenesis.
Two virulence factors for this organism.

questions.model_answer: a) Klebsiella pneumoniae, hypermucoviscous, K1 serotype (positive string test = hypermucoviscosity). b) (1) hematogenous seeding (portal/systemic bacteremia); (2) portal vein pyemia from a bowel/GI source (GI colonization precedes abdominal infection); (3) ascending biliary tract infection from preexisting hepatobiliary disease; (4) direct extension/penetrating trauma. c) (1) polysaccharide capsule (K1) resisting phagocytosis and serum killing; (2) siderophore-based iron acquisition (aerobactin, tonB-regulated).
questions.beyond_mandell: The chapter emphasizes hematogenous/metastatic and GI-colonization routes for KLA; the classic four anatomic routes of pyogenic liver abscess (biliary, portal, arterial/hematogenous, direct) are standard surgical-ID teaching not fully enumerated here.

cohort_answer.text: Organism/serotype: Klebsiella pneumoniae hypermucoviscous K1 serotype. Mechanisms of liver abscess pathogenesis: Haematogenous spread; Portal vein pyemia; Adjacent biliary tree infection; Direct trauma/penetration. Virulence factors: Thick polysaccharide capsule, siderophore iron acquisition system

questions.question_raw: 14. 45F admitted with fever, weight loss, RUQ pain. Abdominal imaging shows 6 cm liver abscess.

parts.text: Name 4 mechanisms of pathogenesis.
The liver aspirate grows a mucoid Gram-negative lactose fermenter — what is the most likely organism (including species)?
A few days after admission the patient develops a painful and erythematous red eye. What is the likely diagnosis?
Based on your answer in b), what phenotype are you suspicious for?
What is one simple bench-side test you can do to confirm this?

parts_raw.text: a) Name 4 mechanisms of pathogenesis
b) The liver aspirate grows a mucoid Gram negative lactose fermenter - what is most likely organism (including species)?
c) A few days after admission, patient develops painful and erythematous red eye. What is the likely diagnosis?
d) Based on your answer in b), what phenotype are you suspicious for?
e) What is one simple benchside test you can do to confirm this?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Biliary (ascending cholangitis/obstruction). (2) Portal venous (pylephlebitis). (3) Hepatic arterial/hematogenous. (4) Direct/contiguous extension or penetrating trauma. b) Klebsiella pneumoniae (hypermucoviscous, capsular serotype K1). c) Endophthalmitis — a metastatic complication of invasive K. pneumoniae liver abscess (metastatic infection, including endophthalmitis, occurs in 10%–16%). d) Hypermucoviscous (hypervirulent) phenotype. e) String test — a positive test is formation of a viscous mucoid string >5 mm when a loop is stretched from a colony on agar.
questions.beyond_mandell: The bedside string test (>5 mm mucoid string) is standard hypermucoviscosity testing not explicitly described in this Mandell slice.

cohort_answer.text: Mechanisms: hepatic artery, portal vein, trauma, biliary tree, contiguous (pleural/intestinal). Organism: Klebsiella pneumoniae. Red eye diagnosis: endophthalmitis as metastatic complication of Kleb. pneumoniae (~12% reported incidence). Phenotype: Hypermucoviscous KP. Benchside test: String test - viscous string >5mm in length by stretching bacterial colonies on agar plate

parts.text: Name 4 mechanisms of liver abscess development.
Abscess culture shows Gram-negative bacilli and the plate shows a positive string test. Name the organism and serotype.
Name two virulence factors for this organism.

parts_raw.text: Name 4 mechanisms of liver abscess development.
Abscess culture shows Gram negative bacilli. Photo shows a blood agar plate with positive string test. Name the organism and serotype.
Name two virulence factors for this organism

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Biliary (ascending cholangitis/obstruction). (2) Portal venous seeding (pylephlebitis). (3) Hepatic arterial/hematogenous seeding. (4) Direct/contiguous extension or penetrating trauma. b) Hypermucoviscous Klebsiella pneumoniae, capsular serotype K1 (occasionally K2). c) (1) Capsular polysaccharide (K1 CPS; magA-directed hypermucoviscosity confers resistance to phagocytosis and serum killing). (2) Regulator of mucoid phenotype protein RmpA and the aerobactin iron-acquisition system, encoded on the large virulence plasmid pLVPK.

cohort_answer.text: Mechanisms: Hematogenous (hepatic arterial blood, portal blood supply), contiguous extension (from gallbladder/biliary tree, from pleural space), percutaneous/penetrating trauma. Organism: Hypermucoviscous Klebsiella pneumoniae, most commonly capsular serotype K1 (or K2 rarely); endemic to SE Asia, Japan, Taiwan, commonly males >60. Virulence factors: capsular polysaccharide, biofilm formation, siderophore for iron acquisition, fimbrial/non-fimbrial adhesion genes, surface polysaccharides RmpA and RmpA2, multidrug resistance, LPS

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Biliary (cholangitis/obstruction). (2) Portal venous (pylephlebitis). (3) Hepatic arterial/hematogenous. (4) Direct/contiguous extension or penetrating trauma. b) Klebsiella pneumoniae, hypermucoviscous capsular serotype K1 (occasionally K2). c) magA (mucoviscosity-associated gene A), which directs K1 capsular polysaccharide synthesis; its mutation abolishes hypermucoviscosity. d) (1) Capsular polysaccharide (antiphagocytic, anti-complement). (2) Iron-acquisition siderophore system (e.g. aerobactin); the regulator RmpA is also recognized.
questions.beyond_mandell: General (non-HMV) Klebsiella virulence factors such as fimbrial adhesins and LPS are established knowledge but not itemized in this Mandell slice.

cohort_answer.text:
Biliary tree (40-50%) – cholangitis abscesses (anaerobes are infrequent); Portal vein (5-15%) – diverticulitis, pancreatitis, IBD, postop IAI pyelphlebitis; Hepatic artery (5-10%) – intravascular infections (IE, line sepsis), micro abscesses; Direct extension from contiguous focus of infection (5-10%) – cholecystitis, perinephric, subphrenic; Penetrating trauma (0-5%) from outside; Cryptogenic (20-40%) mostly in pts with risk factors (DM, cardiopulmonary disease, cirrhosis, malignancy), Job's syndrome, Hemochromatosis (Y. pestis liver abscesses)
Klebsiella pneumoniae – hypermucoid strain (K1 >>>> K2)
magA; rmpA

parts.text: Is there any way to differentiate amoebic from pyogenic abscess clinically?

parts_raw.text: A) Any way to differentiate amoebic vs pyogenic clinically?

questions.model_answer: Clinical criteria alone cannot reliably distinguish them — there is near-complete overlap in symptoms. Features favouring amoebic etiology (from one series) are age ≤45, diarrhea, and a solitary right-lobe abscess. A presumptive diagnosis of amoebic abscess rests on positive E. histolytica serology (EIA ~95% sensitive) with a space-occupying lesion on imaging; otherwise aspiration is used to exclude pyogenic abscess.

cohort_answer.text: Not reliable. Need abscess aspiration. Serology

questions.question_raw:
Q50 (2017 PM)
Clinical case consistent with Klebsiella pneumoniae K1. Syndrome of Klebsiella pneumoniae pyogenic liver abscess complicated by endophthalmitis or CNS infections

parts.text: Given a resistance profile with ceftriaxone susceptible, meropenem resistant, imipenem intermediate, and aztreonam not tested - what would you use?

parts_raw.text: B) Resistance profile: Ceftriaxone (S), Mero (R), Imipenem (I), Aztreonam not mentioned – what to use?

questions.model_answer: The hypervirulent K1 liver-abscess strain is typically antibiotic-susceptible; with ceftriaxone reported susceptible, treat with an active third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime). The discordant meropenem-resistant/imipenem-intermediate pattern against a ceftriaxone-susceptible isolate is atypical for a true carbapenemase and should prompt confirmatory carbapenem MIC testing before assuming carbapenem resistance. Management also requires parenteral therapy plus drainage of the abscess, and, when endophthalmitis is present, ophthalmology consultation with intravitreal antibiotics.
questions.beyond_mandell: The specific antibiotic choice given this susceptibility profile is a clinical/CLSI judgement; this chapter documents the K1 syndrome and that these strains are typically susceptible (p. 2680).

cohort_answer.text: Hypermucoviscous Klebsiella "destructive tissue abscess syndrome": 1) disease in healthy patients, 2) unusual sites e.g. liver, eye, CSF, 3) metastatic spread, 4) hypermucoviscous phenotype

parts_raw.text: B) [image-based question: culture from the fluid demonstrates colonies on blood agar] Name the organism (genus, species, serotype)

questions.model_answer: Klebsiella pneumoniae, capsular serotype K1 (hypermucoviscous/hypervirulent phenotype) - the classic cause of primary invasive community-acquired liver abscess with propensity for metastatic spread (endophthalmitis, meningitis); a positive string test (viscous string >5 mm) supports the hypermucoviscous phenotype.

questions.question: A woman from Taiwan develops seizures and abdominal pain; CT shows brain and liver abscesses. Gram stain from the liver aspirate shows pus and gram-negative bacilli.
questions.question_raw:
Q52 (2010 PM)
Woman from Taiwan develops seizures and abdominal pain, CT shows brain and liver abscesses. Gram stain from liver aspirate shows pus and GNB

parts.text: State the virulence factors that allow the causative organism to produce this specific clinical picture.

parts_raw.text: B) Virulence factors for organism that cause this specific clinical picture?

questions.model_answer: Organism: hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae causing Klebsiella liver abscess with metastatic (brain abscess/meningitis) spread. Virulence factors: (1) Hypermucoviscous polysaccharide capsule, chiefly serotype K1 (and K2), inhibiting phagocytosis and resisting complement/serum killing, linked to clonal complex CC23 carrying a virulence plasmid. (2) rmpA (regulator of mucoid phenotype) driving the hypermucoviscous string-test-positive phenotype (magA is a K1 marker rather than an independent driver). (3) Aerobactin and other TonB-regulated siderophore iron-acquisition systems supporting invasive/metastatic disease. (4) Types 1 and 3 fimbriae for host-cell adherence.

questions.question: A woman from Taiwan develops seizures and abdominal pain. CT of the abdomen and head shows brain abscess and liver abscesses. Gram stain from the liver abscess shows pus and gram-negative bacilli.
questions.question_raw: Q59 (2010 PM). Woman from Taiwan develops seizures and abdominal pain. Has CT scans of abdomen and head which shows brain abscess and liver abscesses. Gram stain from liver abscess shows pus and GNB.

parts.text: What is the most likely organism?
State the virulence factors that allow this organism to cause this specific clinical picture.
What is the treatment?

parts_raw.text: A) What is the most likely organism?
B) Virulence factors for organism to cause this specific picture?
C) Treatment?

questions.model_answer: a) Hypervirulent (hypermucoviscous) Klebsiella pneumoniae, serotype K1/K2, causing Klebsiella liver abscess with metastatic spread. b) (1) Hypermucoviscous K1/K2 capsule inhibiting phagocytosis and resisting bactericidal serum factors; (2) rmpA-driven mucoid phenotype (K1 clonal complex CC23 virulence plasmid); (3) aerobactin and other TonB-regulated siderophore iron-acquisition systems promoting invasive/metastatic disease; (4) types 1 and 3 fimbriae for adherence. c) Source control with drainage of the liver abscess when feasible, plus prolonged parenteral antibiotics directed by susceptibilities; for non-MDR strains options include a beta-lactam such as a third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone), penicillin/beta-lactamase-inhibitor combinations, TMP-SMX, fluoroquinolones, or aminoglycosides (note all K. pneumoniae are intrinsically ampicillin-resistant). Evaluate for metastatic foci; if endophthalmitis is present, urgent ophthalmology consultation with intravitreal antibiotics.

cohort_answer.text: A) Hypermucoviscous Klebsiella pneumoniae. B) Produces mucoviscous exopolysaccharide web resistant to complement-mediated serum killing; polysaccharide capsule; mucoid phenotype inhibiting phagocytosis; LPS; fimbria/pili for adherence. C) Drain abscess if amenable; antibiotics based on susceptibilities (typically Ceftriaxone or Cipro) x4-6 weeks until radiographical resolution.
